extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent agents, patentees and law officers (UK practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on (1) when and how specifications may be amended or disclaimed without enlarging the original invention, and (2) the procedure, evidential requirements, and accounting standards for petitions to extend (prolong) the term of a British patent before the Privy Council/Judicial Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment must not enlarge or materially vary original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: No amendment shall be allowed that would make the specification as amended claim an invention substantially larger than or substantially different from the invention claimed by the specification as it stood before the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is the duty of the Comptroller and law officers, when hearing applications for leave to amend, to see that the proposed amendment does not extend the scope of the patent, or alter the claims such that the invention would become substantially larger or different; if doubtful, amendment ought to be allowed 'at the patentee's peril.' (References: s.18(8) of Patents Act 1883; Iffath and Frost's Patent; Lake's Patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer may sever subordinate part claims but cannot create new claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a specification claims both a general combination and some subordinate parts, a disclaimer may sever and reject the claim to any of the parts; but a specification cannot be altered so as to be made to claim a combination or parts if they were not previously claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee cannot strike out a whole claim and insert another claim to a subordinate part where the original contained a distinct and specific claim to the operation believed to be new. (Illustration: Surry's Patent, 6 R.P.C. 108; Gaulard & Gibbs; United Horseshoe Co. v. Swedish Horsenail Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare disclaimer so sufficient of the invention remains to support the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing a disclaimer care should be taken that sufficient of the invention is left to support the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a disclaimer removes too much so that nothing remains to support the patent, the amendment will fail. (Cases: Gaulard and Gibbs's Patent; United Horseshoe Co. v. Swedish Horsenail Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims can be limited by disclaimer to the particular method described
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a claim to all methods of effecting a certain result, it may be cut down by disclaimer to the particular method described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ashworth's Patent, 2 Griff. P.C. 6 — general method claim narrowed to the specific method disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer must not convert an impracticable generality into a valid specific process
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer is bad which is in effect an attempt to turn a specification for an impracticable generality into a grant for a specific process not sufficiently described originally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the specific successful means were not described in the original specification (only generally involved), limiting by disclaimer to the later-discovered specific mode is improper because the original did not comply with the patent condition of particularly describing the invention. (Ualtrant v. Smith / Lord Chelmsford's reasoning.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller/law officer duty on doubtful amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is clear that a proposed amendment would contravene statutory prohibition, the Comptroller must disallow it; but where the question is doubtful he ought to allow the patentee to make the amendment at his peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretionary approach balances preventing unlawful enlargement with allowing patentees a chance where the statutory compliance is uncertain. (Iffath and Frost's Patent; Lake's Patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Master of the Rolls powers to allow amendments despite s.18
rubrics_metrics.description: The Master of the Rolls has power to allow amendments in a specification filed under the Act of 1852, or which is otherwise to be considered a record under the authority of the M. R., notwithstanding s.18 of the Patents Act 1883.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case reference: Gares Patent, L. R. 26 Ch. D. 105. The M.R. may also order removal of disclaimers filed without patentee's consent (Re Berdan's Patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for correcting clerical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications to amend clerical errors in a specification must be made to the Master of the Rolls or the Comptroller as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several old-law cases demonstrate the practice (e.g., Ashcroft's Patent; Re Redmund; Re Mulberry's Patent; Re Ditmore; Re Munro's Patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller has no statutory power to award costs (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Acts do not authorise the Comptroller to award costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the law officer is empowered by s.38 of the Patents Act 1883 to order costs to be paid by either party where leave to amend is opposed; such orders may be made a rule of Court. Usual practice is to let costs follow the event, discretionary on circumstances. (Practice: Law Officers' Rules nos. 11 and 14; Pittclmann's Patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may petition for extension / timing of petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee, and in some cases an assignee, may petition Her Majesty in Council for prolongation; the petition must be presented at least six months before the patent's expiration (though owners of patents existing before Jan 1, 1884 could apply any time before expiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisements in the public prints must precede petition as required by Privy Council Rules. Assignees may apply but are less favourably regarded unless they assisted the inventor with funds. (Cases: Claridge's Patent; Norton's Patent; Houghton; Napier; Church's Patents.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat/oppose extension and notice rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may enter a caveat at the Registrar of the Council against the extension; caveator is entitled to notice of special application and hearing and may be heard in opposition; caveat must be in the name of the actual opponent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Privy Council Rules, caveators must, within a fortnight after service of copies of the petition, lodge notice of grounds; particulars need not be detailed if grounds are given. Crown may adduce evidence irrespective of objections. (Rules & cases: Lowe's Patent; Ball's Patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition must state all material facts clearly and candidly
rubrics_metrics.description: All facts material to the petitioner's title and to the history of the patent must be stated in the petition; it should be a clear and candid statement of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of material facts can lead to postponement, direction to amend, or refusal/dismissal. Mortgagees and legal personal representatives in certain circumstances must be joined. (Cases: Johnson's Patent; Hutchison's Patent; Mitchell's Patent; Church's Patents; Willacy's R. P.C. 690.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Document filing requirements before hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must lodge specified documents at Privy Council Office prior to hearing: at least one week before the hearing six printed copies of specification and four copies of accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accounts are not filed in due time, Committee may refuse to go into the question. (Privy Council Rules; Johnson's and Atkinson's Patents.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential standard for invention and utility at hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must be prepared with evidence to show that there is an invention, and that the invention possesses utility — meaning substantial merit and usefulness to the public (not merely a scintilla).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also must show that all reasonable means had been taken to make the invention productive; if claiming unreimbursed expenses, must give reasonable evidence of the amount of loss. Utility and merit ought to be shown by testimony of persons of experience and weight. (Cases: Willacy; Stoney; Willacy's Patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show efforts made to bring the invention into use
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner must show that the parties interested had made efforts to bring the invention into public use; prolonged delay in attempting to bring into use without reasonable excuse is a ground for refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to bring into use despite earnest endeavours is a strong presumption of lack of practical utility unless satisfactorily explained (cases cited: Snuthenorth's Patent; Kollman's; Jones'; etc.). Excuses may include incapacity due to accident, inability to raise funds, or strong trade opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate reasonable probability of increased use or sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner should be prepared with evidence to show there is a reasonable probability of an increased use or sale in the immediate future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps justify extension where past profits were inadequate but potential recovery is foreseeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opponents may adduce evidence on novelty/utility/imperfection/specification defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Those opposing the extension may adduce evidence to show the invention lacks novelty or utility, or that it is imperfect, and may point out defects in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient to state grounds of objection without particulars. However, the Committee traditionally avoids deciding novelty/utility unless the patent appears manifestly bad or merit has not been established. (Cases: Ball's Patent; Saxby's Patent; Stewart's Patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of subsequent improvements by others and variation in working
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements by others after the date of the patentee's patent do not by themselves bar extension if the original has merit and the patentee hasn't reaped a benefit proportionate to that merit; variation in manner of working since filing is not a valid ground for refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But if the invention as originally specified proved a failure, or only became successful due to improvements introduced by others, patentee may be disentitled to extension. (Cases: Galloway; Napier; Woodcraft; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing litigation and treatment of patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: If litigation involving the validity of the patent is ongoing at the time of application, the Committee will not generally go into the question but will assume the patent to be valid unless a court has decided against validity or invalidity is beyond reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a competent tribunal later decides the original patent invalid, the new patent/extension will share the same fate. Where validity is doubtful but good grounds for extension exist, extension may still be granted. (Cases: general citations including Kay's Patent; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy prohibition on pre-arranged exclusive licence to obtain extension
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for prolongation will be refused where the patentee has agreed by deed with a public company to grant an exclusive licence and covenanted to obtain prolongation for the same purpose, as contrary to public policy and repugnant to the statute's spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: Cardwell's Patent (10 Moore P.C.C. 488).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounts must be full, clear, unreserved and strictly proved
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the petitioner's duty to satisfy the Committee beyond controversy as to what remuneration the invention has brought him, by producing accounts that leave no doubt as to receipts and payments connected with the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts not filed or unsatisfactory may lead to refusal or require reference to account-taking by decree; late applications to amend accounts at hearing are likely to be refused; examples: Saxby's Patent; Yates & Kellett; Johnson & Atkinson; Markwick; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep patent accounts distinct and include profits from every branch
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee should keep accounts under the patent distinct from other business; profits of every branch connected with the patented invention (including subsidiary manufacture used as feeder) must be set forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patent exploited via company, the company's accounts should be deposited. Profits year-by-year and profits made abroad under foreign patents must be shown. Failure to distinguish patent expenditure from other business can lead to dismissal. (Cases: Nobel's Explosives Company; Deacon's Patent; Perkins' Patent; Hardy's Patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain absence of books or inability to show profits; failure may disentitle
rubrics_metrics.description: If books of account are not forthcoming the petitioner must explain their absence; if the patentee's dealing with rights prevents showing amounts received by working the patent or licensees, he may be considered disentitled to extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Markwick's Patent; Trotman's Patent; Saxby's Patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted deductions from profits when assessing remuneration
rubrics_metrics.description: In taking an account of profits and loss the patentee is entitled to charge for personal expenses and loss of time devoted to the patent, travelling expenses, salaries of clerks, commissions on sales where he acted as salesman, and cost of making experiments; law expenses in maintaining rights are generally allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial practice varies as to allowing manufacturer's profits deductions and proportions; compromises giving up costs may bar deduction; new deductions not mentioned in petition/accounts are inadmissible at the hearing. (Cases: Trotman's; Kay's; Bailey's; Hill's Patent; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient or non-distinguishing accounts lead to dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions will be dismissed where accounts are insufficient, e.g., not distinguishing expenditure on the part of the invention proved useful or failing to bring accounts in a satisfactory form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Willacy's Patent; Yates & Kellett; Yates application to amend accounts refused at hearing. Petitioners should present complete, separate, and properly vouched accounts.
